doc.title: Ralph Humphrey interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Studio work in Los Angeles and leaving the road
summary: Humphrey describes what a studio player must be, how studio work curtailed road work, and his path from Ellis to Zappa, Seals & Crofts and the studios by 1976.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well you got into the studio scene in Los Angeles?
Well when you were doing it.

Yeah. I kind of always felt at some point that I would want to do that because I felt I had all the right tools for it. My reading was really good, I felt like I had a familiarity with all the styles, I was responsible for all the things that one needs to be responsible for in that position—

Well you know taking command, being able to follow the click, being able to take the right instruction, follow a conductor, take suggestions without fighting back, so being diplomatic about the situation because it’s not your gig it’s somebody else’s gig and you’re being privileged to be there doing the work and so you try to do the best job that you know how. And I felt that I really had the make-up to do all that. It’s sort of a self confidence about your ability because you don’t want to be at all concerned about your inability to do something if you’re in a studio because it’ll show you the door real quick, particularly in the rhythm section. Not too many people get away with less than really good playing in the studios. So it’s all the top notch people. And I guess I had some sort of — it’s kind of a glorification of being a musician and doing that kind of work, that

high quality of work. And it’s kind of a trade off because in order to be available for that kind of work you really can’t be doing something else, full time anyhow, because you’ll not be called. I mean if you’re gone, you’re gone. And they don’t think about you anymore. So you know you’ve got to sort of play that game and you think can I leave town for a couple of weeks and still be okay? So it curtailed my road career.
That’s so funny because — I mean it’s not funny except that Ernie Watts told me the same exact thing. It’s like if you’re gone for a week, people like — well he’s gone.

Yeah. Right. So you know you sneak out of town and do this and do that and then you get back into town and nobody knows you went. But it would be difficult to try to lead more than one life at a time. So I chose to try to stay in town after I sort of took myself off the road, which was after — well I played Don’s band off and on for five years, and then joined Frank Zappa’s Mothers of Invention for a couple of years, and then went out some more and did a little sort of more rock-pop stuff, Seals & Crofts and a few other people, and then by 1976 the studios were looking attractive to me and I wanted to sort of become a homebody a little bit. So I had opportunities to stay on the road but I dismissed them and came home, started a recording career, a studio career.
